extracted.intended_audience: researchers preparing NIH-style Specific Aims pages (e.g., R01, K awards); grant applicants and mentors reviewing aims pages
extracted.subtask_description: Create a standalone, one-page Specific Aims document using a four-paragraph structure that succinctly states the problem, gap, objective, approach, and discrete aims with expected outcomes and significance for an NIH-style grant application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall structure: one-page standalone
rubrics_metrics.description: The specific aims page is a standalone, one-page document that succinctly conveys your research idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be well organized with good use of white space, bold, and underline. The page should be readable independently of the rest of the application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four-paragraph structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize the page into four paragraphs: (1) Hook/Introduction, (2) Critical Need/Knowledge Gap, (3) Approach Overview/Rationale, (4) The Aims (numbered list), plus a brief closing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the recommended lengths for each paragraph and use the numbered Aims list for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph 1 — Hook / Introduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Set up the scientific problem in broad terms a non-expert can understand: topic and importance (1-2 sentences), current state of knowledge (1-2 sentences), the pivotal gap that prevents progress. End with a sentence that states the gap or problem (often: 'However, [the critical gap]...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep this to 3-5 sentences; prioritize clarity for non-expert reviewers and end with an explicit statement of the critical gap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph 2 — Critical need / Knowledge gap
rubrics_metrics.description: State the critical need: what is needed to fill the gap; long-term goal of your research program; the objective of THIS application; the central hypothesis (if hypothesis-driven); justification for your hypothesis (preliminary data + literature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 3-5 sentences. Make explicit what this application will accomplish and how it fits into a broader research program; cite preliminary data briefly to justify the hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph 3 — Approach overview / Rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: Summarize your approach to test the hypothesis, why you are well-positioned to do the work (preliminary data, expertise), and briefly mention methods/innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 3-4 sentences. Convey feasibility and competence without excess methodological detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph 4 — The Aims (numbered list)
rubrics_metrics.description: List each Aim with a short title and the standard Aim format: Aim title (active verb + key concept); Hypothesis (if applicable); Approach (brief methods); Expected outcome (what you'll learn).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each aim should be concise, clearly tied to the central objective/hypothesis, and include expected outcomes. Use the Aim template (Aim X: [Title]  *Hypothesis*: ...  *Approach*: ...  *Expected outcome*: ...).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim wording: begin with 'To ...' and include why
rubrics_metrics.description: Each aim should start with 'To xxx' where xxx is WHY you are doing the Aim, then continue with a verb + WHAT you are going to do to test your hypothesis for that Aim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the first phrase of the Aim communicate purpose (why), followed by an active verb describing the experiment/analysis (what).

rubrics_metrics.name: Closing: significance / impact
rubrics_metrics.description: End with 1-2 sentences emphasizing the significance/impact of expected outcomes (e.g., 'Successful completion of these aims will ...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tie expected outcomes back to the big-picture impact and how this work departs from the status quo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use strong, active language
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer assertive Active constructions such as 'We will determine,' 'We will establish,' 'We will characterize' and avoid hedging such as 'We hope to,' 'We will attempt to,' 'We will try'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use confident, definitive verbs to signal feasibility and commitment; remove hedging qualifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word economy
rubrics_metrics.description: Every sentence must work; be concise and cut hedging, redundancy, and unnecessary qualifiers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target one page ≈ 500–800 words depending on figures. Edit ruthlessly: eliminate filler words and tighten phrasing to make each sentence carry essential information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual elements: consider a simple figure
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider adding a figure (conceptual model, hypothesis schematic). Simple figures save words and provide visual reinforcement but don't overcrowd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you include a figure, make it simple and directly clarifying; balance figure space against word economy so the page remains readable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence of aims
rubrics_metrics.description: Aims should NOT be co-dependent; one aim should not require success of another. Each aim should have a discrete falsifiable hypothesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design aims so that failure of one aim does not invalidate the others; ensure each aim can produce interpretable results on its own.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common aim structures / sequencing
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested aim progressions include: (1) Test hypothesis A; (2) Test hypothesis B (related but independent); (3) Apply findings (e.g., translation, model). OR (1) Define mechanism; (2) Identify regulators; (3) Test perturbation effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select an aim structure that logically advances from discovery/definition to mechanism to application/translation as appropriate for the project.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewers look for: clear statement of significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers expect a clear statement of significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state why the problem matters and how the proposed outcomes will shift the field or address an important need.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewers look for: compelling rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers want a compelling rationale for the proposed work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Connect the gap to your approaches and preliminary data; explain why your plan is the logical next step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewers look for: achievable within the project period
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers evaluate whether the aims are achievable in 4–5 years (or the relevant funding period).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scope aims realistically and justify feasibility with preliminary data, timelines, and methods that match the funding period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewers look for: strong investigator/team (implied)
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong investigator/team is something reviewers look for (this may be implied on the Aims page).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Briefly indicate your position, relevant expertise, and preliminary data to signal that the team can execute the plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewers look for: innovative but feasible
rubrics_metrics.description: Work should be innovative while remaining feasible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight novelty but pair it with achievable methods and preliminary support to avoid being judged as speculative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewers look for: measurable endpoints
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide measurable endpoints so reviewers can see how success will be assessed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State expected outcomes and specific measurable endpoints or criteria for each Aim where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common mistake: aims that are descriptive rather than hypothesis-driven
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid aims that are purely descriptive and not hypothesis-driven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame aims so they test hypotheses or answer specific mechanistic questions rather than only cataloging observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common mistake: hedging language
rubrics_metrics.description: Hedging language signals lack of confidence and should be removed (e.g., 'we hope to', 'we will attempt').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use strong, active language to convey confidence and feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common mistake: co-dependent aims
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid co-dependent aims where success of one aim is required for another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Redesign aims to be independently interpretable or include contingency plans to minimize co-dependency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common mistake: too ambitious / unrealistic scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not propose aims that are overly ambitious or unrealistic for the funding period and resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scale aims to match time, personnel, and resources; prioritize achievable milestones and measurable endpoints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common mistake: insufficient context for non-expert reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to provide sufficient context for non-expert reviewers reduces clarity and impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain the problem and gap in accessible language early in the page; avoid jargon without explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common mistake: missing significance / 'so what'
rubrics_metrics.description: Not stating the significance or the 'so what' of the proposed work is a frequent flaw.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly connect expected outcomes to field impact, translational relevance, or how they address the stated gap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common mistake: no mention of preliminary data
rubrics_metrics.description: Omitting any mention of preliminary data undermines justification for feasibility and hypothesis support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Briefly reference key preliminary data or prior work that supports feasibility and the central hypothesis.
